name: M-Lab NDT server, ndt7 client and MSAK
purpose: Open server and client implementations of the Network Diagnostic Tool (ndt7) and the multi-stream MSAK test, plus the published M-Lab dataset of billions of throughput measurements.
journalism_use_case: Evidence for throttling and degradation stories — the slow-lane variant of a shutdown, where connectivity technically persists but collapses in throughput — and for long-run comparisons of network performance by ISP and region, which is how you show that a specific provider degraded a specific service.
pros: The published M-Lab dataset is an enormous longitudinal record of real client measurements, which makes before-and-after throttling claims quantifiable rather than anecdotal
Apache-2.0 across the stack with the server runnable yourself if you want controlled measurements from known vantage points
Active maintenance (v0.26.1 released 2026-10-15, same-day push) under a long-standing institutional programme
Open data publication model means your analysis can be reproduced by a reader or a regulator
cons: This is performance measurement, not censorship detection: it will not tell you a site is blocked, only that a path is degraded, and attributing degradation to deliberate throttling needs corroboration you must supply

M-Lab publishes results openly including truncated client IP and ASN — a documented and deliberate design choice, but it means measurements are not private and a client on a small network may be identifiable
88 open issues and a multi-repository ecosystem (server, clients, MSAK, data pipelines) that takes orientation effort
Throughput measurement is noisy: client-side conditions (wifi, device, congestion) confound ISP-level conclusions, so single tests prove nothing
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the open publication of results including truncated client IP and ASN is stated by M-Lab; 137 stars with 88 open issues; release v0.26.1 on 2026-10-15. M-Lab data has been used in regulatory and journalistic analysis of broadband performance, which is credible usage context.
assessment: Useful for a specific and under-covered story type — throttling rather than blocking — where it is close to the only open evidence source. For your profile the realistic use is analysing the published dataset rather than running servers: pull per-ASN throughput time series around a disputed event and look for the discontinuity. Be rigorous about confounders, and be aware that encouraging readers to run tests produces measurements published with their truncated IP and ASN.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-15, latest release v0.26.1 published the same day, 137 stars, 88 open issues. Regular releases under a funded institutional programme with an operating server fleet.
model_or_data_licence: M-Lab publishes its measurement dataset openly (CC-BY-style per M-Lab's data policy — verify current terms before bulk redistribution).
costs: No fee. Analysing the published dataset via BigQuery incurs Google Cloud query charges (usage-based; current rates not verified here). Running your own NDT server is a modest VM plus bandwidth. Estimate.
privacy: Tests measure the client's own connection, and M-Lab publishes results openly including truncated client IP and ASN — a documented trade-off in favour of open data. Anyone you ask to run a test should be told their network is published. Querying the dataset exposes your analysis interest to Google.
alternatives: OONI for blocking rather than degradation
RIPE Atlas for latency and reachability from fixed vantage points
Cloudflare Radar or ISP-published data for corroboration, with their own terms
summary: Open server and client implementations of the Network Diagnostic Tool (ndt7) and the multi-stream MSAK test…

name: RIPE Atlas tooling (Magellan CLI, Cousteau, Sagan)
purpose: Command-line client and Python libraries for scheduling and retrieving RIPE Atlas measurements — ping, traceroute, DNS, TLS, HTTP — from a global fleet of volunteer-hosted hardware probes.
journalism_use_case: Lets a reporter schedule pings, traceroutes, DNS and TLS measurements from probes inside a specific country or ASN during an unfolding shutdown, and watch probe disconnections as an independent outage signal — measurement from inside the affected network without asking any person there to act.
pros: Measurement from inside the affected country without putting a human there at risk — the probes are already deployed, which is a significant ethical advantage over asking a source to run software
Probe disconnection itself is a usable outage signal, independent of the measurements you schedule
DNS and traceroute from in-country vantage points can distinguish DNS tampering from routing-level blocking, which is the technical detail a story needs
Actively maintained (pushed 2026-10-22, tag v3.4.1) by RIPE NCC with a very clean issue tracker (10 open)
cons: Probe coverage is thin and skewed in exactly the countries that matter most for shutdown reporting — a country may have too few probes to support any claim, and this limitation is systematic rather than occasional
The credit system is a real throttle on sustained measurement: you earn credits by hosting probes or receive an allowance, and heavy measurement exhausts it
Results are by default published publicly in RIPE Atlas, so your measurement activity and targets are visible — an operational-security consideration if the target would object
Release objects lag tags (v3.2.0 published 2025-09-25 against tag v3.4.1), and the CLI assumes familiarity with measurement concepts
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the credit-system throttle and default public publication of results are stated in RIPE Atlas documentation; 218 stars with only 10 open issues, indicating good triage; last push 2026-10-22.
assessment: The ethically cleanest way to measure from inside a hostile network, and for that reason the one I would reach for before commissioning an in-country OONI probe. Two practical cautions: check probe coverage for the target country before planning a story around it, because thin coverage will defeat you; and remember your measurements are public, so scheduling a burst of traceroutes at a government network is a visible act. Pair with PyBGPStream for the routing view.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-22, latest release v3.2.0 (2025-09-25), latest tag v3.4.1, 218 stars, 10 open issues. Low backlog and current commits under RIPE NCC institutional maintenance; release objects trail the tag line.
model_or_data_licence: RIPE Atlas measurement results are published under RIPE NCC's terms (not separately verified here).
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 on the tooling. Note that RIPE Atlas usage is governed by RIPE NCC's acceptable-use terms and the credit system, which are service conditions rather than licence terms.
costs: No software fee. Measurement is throttled by RIPE Atlas credits: you earn them by hosting a probe or anchor, or receive a starting allowance. Sustained measurement realistically requires hosting probes — a hardware and bandwidth cost rather than a licence fee. Current credit rates were not verified in this survey.
privacy: Measurements are initiated by you from third-party probes and, by default, results are published publicly in RIPE Atlas — so both your targets and your measurement pattern are visible. Probe hosts are volunteers whose networks are already exposed by participation; you are not adding risk to them, but you are acting visibly.
alternatives: OONI Probe where application-layer blocking rather than reachability is the question
PyBGPStream for the control-plane view with no measurement footprint
IODA for a pre-computed outage answer
blockers: Thin probe coverage in many high-interest countries; measurements are public by default
summary: Command-line client and Python libraries for scheduling and retrieving RIPE Atlas measurements — ping, traceroute, DNS, TLS…

name: Internet Health Report (IHR)
maintainer: Internet Health Report project (IIJ Research Lab and collaborators)
purpose: Platform computing and publishing per-AS and per-country internet health indicators — AS hegemony (transit dependency), delay and forwarding anomalies, link congestion — from public measurement and routing data.
journalism_use_case: Useful for the attribution half of a shutdown story: showing which upstream autonomous system a country depends on, and therefore which operator or transit provider is the chokepoint when connectivity drops. That turns 'the internet went down' into 'this specific operator was the single point of control'.
pros: AS hegemony is a genuinely distinctive metric for journalism: it identifies structural chokepoints, which is the precondition for a shutdown being technically possible
Published as a browsable site plus an API, so a reporter can get the dependency picture without running the analysis
GPL-3.0 with the front end actively released (v1.8.8, 2026-10-23)
Combines routing and active-measurement data, so the indicators are not single-source
cons: A research codebase rather than a product: several analysis components (disco, ashash) have been untouched since 2022, so the pipeline behind the published indicators is unevenly maintained

Indicators need expert interpretation — AS hegemony is a statistical dependency measure, not a statement that an operator controls traffic, and over-reading it would produce a wrong attribution in print
Documentation is uneven, and the Kafka-based analysis stack is not realistically deployable by a newsroom
Small community (93 stars) and the site is the only practical interface
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the front end is actively released (v1.8.8, 2026-10-23) while named analysis components have been dormant since 2022 — a split maintenance picture verified from the project's repositories. 93 stars, 3 open issues.
assessment: Use the published site and API for the structural question of who the chokepoints are; do not try to run the pipeline. For your profile the value is specific and real: when a shutdown happens, IHR tells you which operator to put the question to, which is the difference between reporting an outage and reporting a decision. Have the dependency interpretation checked by someone who understands BGP economics before attributing control to a named company.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: ihr-website archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-23, latest release v1.8.8 same day, 93 stars, 3 open issues. However, sibling analysis components (disco, ashash) have not been updated since 2022 per session-1 inspection. Classified stable-low because the public service and front end are current while the analytical back end is partly frozen.
model_or_data_licence: Derived indicators are published on the site; data terms not separately verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 on the website code; irrelevant for using the hosted service.
costs: Free to use. Self-hosting the full analysis would require RIPE Atlas and BGP data feeds plus a Kafka cluster — not a realistic newsroom cost, so no estimate is offered.
privacy: Processes public network measurement and routing data into aggregate per-AS and per-country indicators; no end-user data is involved and browsing runs no measurement.
alternatives: PyBGPStream to compute dependency relationships yourself from public archives
IODA for the outage event itself
RIPEstat for simpler AS relationship lookups
summary: Platform computing and publishing per-AS and per-country internet health indicators — AS hegemony (transit dependency)…

name: Internet Society Pulse
purpose: Hosted dashboard aggregating third-party measurement sources into country-level views of internet shutdowns, resilience, enabling technologies and market concentration, with a shutdown timeline.
journalism_use_case: A no-code entry point for a reporter who needs a credible country shutdown timeline and citable summary figures in minutes, without running or interpreting raw measurements — the fastest route to a defensible number for a deadline piece.
pros: Fastest path from question to citable figure for a non-technical reporter, with an institutional name (Internet Society) behind the attribution
The shutdown timeline is curated, so it provides context and precedent that raw measurement data does not
Draws on multiple upstream measurement providers (OONI, IODA, M-Lab and others), so figures are not single-source
cons: Classified adjacent rather than open source: the dashboard's code is not public and the one public repository (pulse-data) carries no licence, with 0 stars and 0 open issues — so reuse terms are unverified and self-hosting is impossible
Figures are derived from other people's measurements, so you are citing a secondary source — for a contested claim you should go to the primary data (OONI, IODA) and cite that instead
No API-level guarantees or published methodology depth comparable to the primary projects, so reproducing a figure can be difficult
Dependency risk: a hosted dashboard can change its methodology or disappear, and your published figure cannot then be reproduced
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the public pulse-data repository has no licence, 0 stars and 0 open issues, and the dashboard code is not published — verified via the GitHub API on 2026-11-17. The dashboard itself is live and maintained by the Internet Society.
assessment: Use it as a starting point and a sanity check, not as your citation. For your profile the right habit is to find the figure on Pulse, then trace it back to OONI or IODA and cite the primary measurement with a permalink — that way the claim survives both official denial and the dashboard changing. Reserve direct Pulse citation for context and precedent rather than for the central factual claim of a story.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: InternetSociety/pulse-data archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-19, no releases, no detected licence, 0 stars, 0 open issues. The dashboard is live but its code is not public, so repository-based maintenance assessment is not possible. Classified Uncertain deliberately rather than assuming continuity from the organisation's reputation.
licence: Not verified — dashboard code is not public; the public pulse-data repository carries no licence file
model_or_data_licence: Upstream measurement providers' terms apply to the underlying data; Pulse's own presentation terms were not verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: Unverified. Do not assume figures may be redistributed as a dataset; cite and link rather than republish.
costs: Free to use. No infrastructure. Not self-hostable.
privacy: Presents aggregated public measurement data; visiting the dashboard sends no measurement traffic of your own. Ordinary web-analytics exposure applies.
alternatives: OONI Explorer and IODA for primary, citable measurements
Access Now's shutdown tracking for advocacy-grade timelines with their own terms
Internet Health Report for structural dependency context
blockers: Code not public and public repository unlicensed — reuse terms unverified, not self-hostable
summary: Hosted dashboard aggregating third-party measurement sources into country-level views of internet shutdowns, resilience…
oss_detail: Hosted service or proprietary software — governed by service terms, not a software licence

name: changedetection.io
purpose: Self-hosted web-page change-detection service with CSS/XPath region selection, text and visual comparison, a browser-based fetcher for JavaScript-heavy pages, and notifications via Apprise to email, Slack, Discord and dozens of other channels.
journalism_use_case: Watch specific regions of agency pages, FOIA logs, press-release indexes or policy PDFs and get an alert with a diff when the wording quietly changes — the standard way a small newsroom notices that a government rewrote a page rather than announcing a change.
pros: Region selection via CSS or XPath is what makes it usable on real government pages: you can watch the one table that matters and ignore the rotating banner that would otherwise fire alerts daily
Largest community in this subcategory by a wide margin (35,859 stars) with frequent releases (0.70.3, 2026-11-09) — genuinely maintained rather than a weekend project
Self-hosted with snapshots and diffs stored locally, and notifications routed wherever you choose
Browser fetcher handles JavaScript-rendered portals that defeat simple HTTP watchers
cons: Per-URL watch model with no built-in editorial triage or annotation workflow, so a newsroom watching hundreds of pages has no way to separate reviewed from unreviewed changes — EDGI's platform exists precisely for that gap
JS-heavy or bot-protected government portals may still block the fetcher, and diagnosing that is fiddly
Frequent releases mean upgrade churn: 386 open issues and rapid version movement make pinning important
Notification payloads can include page text, so an alert routed to a third-party service (Slack, Discord, email provider) discloses the monitored content to that provider
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. The quantitative signals are strong and checkable: 35,859 stars with 386 open issues and a release on 2026-11-09 — a large, active user base with a correspondingly large support load. Widely recommended in web-monitoring tool lists including EDGI's.
assessment: My default recommendation for a small newsroom that wants page monitoring working this week. Two configuration decisions matter for your context: route notifications to an internal channel rather than a third-party chat service if the monitored pages are sensitive, and pin the version because the release cadence will otherwise surprise you. When the watch list grows past what one person can triage, graduate to EDGI's platform rather than adding more watches here.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 0.70.3 (2026-11-09), 35,859 stars, 386 open issues. Frequent point releases and daily commits; the large backlog reflects scale of use rather than neglect.
licence_restrictions: None material. Note the project also sells a hosted version — that is a separate service under its own terms, not a licence restriction on the self-hosted code.
costs: No fee for self-hosting. Infrastructure estimate: a small container; add a Playwright/Chromium container for JS-heavy pages, which roughly doubles the resource footprint. The project's hosted service is priced separately and was not verified in this survey. Operating effort is low.
privacy: Snapshots and diffs stay in your self-hosted instance. The exposure point is notifications: payloads can include page text, so routing alerts through Slack, Discord or an external email provider discloses monitored content to them. Choose an internal channel for sensitive watches.
alternatives: urlwatch or webchanges for a CLI, version-controlled watchlist
Klaxon for a reporter-facing point-and-click interface
EDGI web-monitoring-db when the watch list exceeds informal triage
summary: Self-hosted web-page change-detection service with CSS/XPath region selection, text and visual comparison…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: urlwatch
purpose: Command-line tool that fetches URLs or runs shell commands on a schedule, applies filters to normalise the content, and reports diffs via email, Slack, Matrix, stdout and other backends.
journalism_use_case: Script a reproducible watchlist of statute, regulation or guidance pages in version control, and receive diffs by email, Slack, Matrix or stdout when an official page is edited — the engineer's answer to monitoring, where the watchlist itself is reviewable as code.
pros: Configuration as code means your watchlist is version-controlled and reviewable, which is a genuine methodological advantage over a UI-managed list — you can show what you were watching on a given date
Filter pipeline (html2text, jq, CSS selectors, regex) is powerful enough to suppress boilerplate churn that would otherwise drown real changes
Can watch command output, not just URLs, so an API endpoint or a database query becomes monitorable with no extra tooling
Mature and stable with a large user base (3,148 stars) and a small backlog relative to that
cons: CLI and text-first with no web UI or multi-user triage, so it does not scale to a team reviewing changes together
No built-in archiving of the captured snapshot as evidence — you get a diff, not a dated preservation copy, so pair it with a capture tool if the change may be disputed
Four-month gap since last push (2026-07-10) and GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION despite a BSD-3-Clause licence, with no GitHub release objects (latest tag 2.29)
The maintainer has signalled interest in a successor project over the years, so long-term direction is less certain than the install base suggests
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 3,148 stars with 85 open issues; last push 2026-07-10; SPDX NOASSERTION at the API level with the licence resolved to BSD-3-Clause by reading the file (session-1 verification, retained). webchanges exists explicitly as a more actively developed fork-descendant, which is itself a signal about urlwatch's cadence.
assessment: Choose it when you want the watchlist in git and the whole thing auditable — that is a real advantage for a methodology note. But given the four-month quiet period and the existence of webchanges as a more actively developed descendant, I would evaluate webchanges first for a new deployment. Whichever you pick, add a capture step (Scoop or ArchiveBox) so you hold dated evidence of the before state, not just a diff.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-07-10, no GitHub release objects, latest tag 2.29, SPDX NOASSERTION (licence resolved to BSD-3-Clause by file inspection), 3,148 stars, 85 open issues. Four months quiet on a mature, feature-complete tool; not declining, but webchanges is the more active line.
licence: BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE file read directly; GitHub API reports NOASSERTION)
costs: No fee. Runs as a cron job on any small host. Optional Playwright for browser jobs adds resource cost. Negligible.
privacy: Snapshot cache and diffs stay on the local machine; only the configured reporter transmits content off-box. Choosing stdout or a local mailbox keeps everything internal — the most private option in this subcategory.
alternatives: webchanges — the more actively developed descendant, recommended for new deployments
changedetection.io for a UI and visual diffing
shot-scraper plus git for screenshot-and-commit monitoring
summary: Command-line tool that fetches URLs or runs shell commands on a schedule, applies filters to normalise the content…

name: webchanges
purpose: Actively developed descendant of urlwatch that monitors web pages and documents, with HTML-formatted diff reports, PDF and image text extraction, JSON handling, Playwright-based browser fetching and optional AI-generated change summaries.
journalism_use_case: Monitor official documents and dashboards that urlwatch handles poorly — PDF text, images, JSON APIs — and receive readable HTML diffs of what an agency altered. The PDF capability matters because many governments publish changes as new PDFs rather than edited pages.
pros: PDF and image text extraction is the decisive differentiator: monitoring a PDF-published register or guidance document is a common journalism need that most watchers cannot meet
HTML-formatted diff reports are materially easier for a non-engineer to read than urlwatch's text output, so alerts can go to reporters directly
Most actively developed tool in this subcategory by release cadence — v3.40.0 released on 2026-11-15, same-day push
MIT licensed and configuration-as-code, retaining urlwatch's auditability advantage
cons: Effectively a single-maintainer project with a small user base (50 stars) — excellent cadence but a bus factor of one, which matters for a monitoring system you depend on
No web UI or collaborative review, so like urlwatch it does not support team triage

The optional AI summary feature introduces a third-party data-sharing decision: enabling it sends monitored content to an LLM provider, which newsrooms should review before use rather than discover later
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION despite the MIT licence, so compliance records need the file reference
feedback: No individual user reports verified — 50 stars means there is little community signal to report. Documented: release v3.40.0 on 2026-11-15 with same-day push and only 6 open issues, which is an exceptional cadence-to-backlog ratio; the AI-summary feature's third-party dependency is documented by the project.
assessment: My recommendation for a new CLI-based monitoring deployment, ahead of urlwatch, on cadence and PDF support. Two conditions for your context: leave the AI summary feature off unless you have deliberately chosen a self-hosted model endpoint, and accept the single-maintainer risk by keeping your configuration portable — the config format is close enough to urlwatch's that migration is feasible if the project stops.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-15, latest release v3.40.0 published the same day, SPDX NOASSERTION (licence MIT per the repository file), 50 stars, 6 open issues. Frequent releases and a near-empty tracker; the risk is maintainer concentration, not activity.
licence: MIT (repository licence file; GitHub API reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: n/a — the optional AI summary feature uses whichever LLM provider you configure, under that provider's terms.
costs: No fee. Small host; optional Playwright/Chromium adds resources. If the AI summary feature is enabled, you incur that provider's token charges (not priced here). Negligible otherwise.
privacy: Snapshots and diffs are held locally; content leaves the machine only via configured reporters or, if enabled, the AI summary feature — which transmits monitored content to an LLM provider. Treat that feature as off by default for sensitive monitoring.
alternatives: urlwatch for the longer-established, larger-community option
changedetection.io for a web UI and visual diffs
EDGI web-monitoring-db for team-scale triage
summary: Actively developed descendant of urlwatch that monitors web pages and documents, with HTML-formatted diff reports…

name: Klaxon (self-hosted)
purpose: Self-hosted Rails application that lets non-technical users select page elements to watch via a point-and-click browser extension and receive email alerts when the selected content changes.
journalism_use_case: Give reporters without command-line skills a point-and-click way to watch FOIA disclosure logs, court dockets and agency pages and get alerted to newsworthy edits — built by a newsroom for exactly this purpose, which shows in the workflow assumptions.
pros: Built by a working newsroom for reporters, so the selection and alerting flow matches how journalists actually monitor sources — the clearest journalism-native design in this subcategory
The browser-extension selector removes the CSS/XPath barrier entirely, which is the single biggest obstacle to reporters self-serving on monitoring
Watch list, snapshots and diffs live in the newsroom's own PostgreSQL instance, so monitored content stays internal
Still receiving maintenance (pushed 2026-11-16) with 683 stars — the largest community of the newsroom-built options
cons: The README explicitly warns it 'may break unexpectedly' and may miss a change or fail to send mail — an honest disclosure that nonetheless means you cannot rely on absence of an alert
Individual-user support has been discontinued, and recent repository activity is dependency maintenance rather than development, so the project is being kept alive rather than advanced
Rails plus PostgreSQL plus SendGrid or SMTP is a real deployment, and the documented path assumes Heroku — awkward if you self-host elsewhere
Email-only alerting by default (with optional Slack/Discord webhooks), so routing into a newsroom workflow takes extra work
feedback: No individual user reports verified, but the project's own README contains the significant documented caveat — that it may break unexpectedly, miss changes or fail to send mail — and notes that individual-user support is discontinued. 683 stars, 16 open issues, release v0.7.0 (2026-03-09), last push 2026-11-16 consisting of dependency maintenance.
assessment: Valuable for its reporter-facing design and worth deploying if you have Rails capacity and want journalists monitoring their own beats — that self-service property is what makes monitoring actually happen. But take the README's warning seriously: treat it as best-effort notification, never as a guarantee, and pair critical watches with a second tool. If you have no Rails capability, changedetection.io reaches a similar outcome with less deployment friction.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v0.7.0 (2026-03-09), 683 stars, 16 open issues. Recent pushes are dependency maintenance rather than feature work, individual-user support is discontinued per the project, and the README warns of unreliability. Declining rather than dormant: the lights are on, nobody is building.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure estimate: a Rails host plus PostgreSQL, plus an email-sending service (SendGrid or similar — small monthly cost, rates not verified here). Heroku was the documented deployment target, which carries its own hosting charges. Operating effort is moderate.
privacy: Watch list, snapshots and diffs live in your own PostgreSQL instance. Alert emails route through the configured mail provider, which sees the alert content — choose an internal mail path for sensitive watches.
alternatives: changedetection.io — recommended alternative with a UI and much more active maintenance
Klaxon Cloud (DocumentCloud add-on) if you want no infrastructure at all
webchanges where an engineer manages the watchlist on reporters' behalf
blockers: Project's own README warns it may break and may miss changes; individual-user support discontinued
summary: Self-hosted Rails application that lets non-technical users select page elements to watch via a point-and-click browser extension…

name: Klaxon Cloud (DocumentCloud Add-On)
purpose: Hosted reimplementation of Klaxon as a DocumentCloud Add-On, with a browser extension for selecting page regions, scheduled checking via GitHub Actions and Cloudflare Workers, and an Internet Archive snapshot attached to each detected change.
journalism_use_case: Lets a reporter with only a DocumentCloud account monitor web pages for newsworthy edits without running a server, with an Internet Archive snapshot attached as evidence of the before-and-after — which is the one thing self-hosted watchers typically omit.
pros: Zero infrastructure for the newsroom: a reporter with a DocumentCloud account can start monitoring the same day, which is decisive for teams with no engineering capacity
Automatic Internet Archive snapshot per detected change gives you third-party-attested evidence of the before state — a genuine evidentiary advantage over local-diff-only tools
Revives a capability that the self-hosted Klaxon no longer reliably provides, under active MuckRock stewardship (pushed 2026-09-10)
The add-on script itself is BSD-3-Clause, so the automation logic is inspectable
cons: The front-end monorepo carries no licence file, so reuse rights for the extension and site code are not verified — only the add-on script's BSD-3-Clause is confirmed

Hosted model means watch configuration, run history and detected changes live in MuckRock's DocumentCloud infrastructure rather than the newsroom's, with less control over retention — unsuitable for monitoring that should stay confidential
Dependency chain is long and third-party-heavy (DocumentCloud, GitHub Actions, Cloudflare Workers, Internet Archive), so availability depends on several services you do not control
Tiny repository footprint (9 stars, 1 open issue) and no releases, so it is hard to assess independently of MuckRock's operation of it
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the add-on script is BSD-3-Clause while the front-end monorepo has no licence file (verified session 1, retained); 9 stars; last push 2026-09-10. MuckRock operates it as part of the DocumentCloud Add-On ecosystem.
assessment: The right recommendation for a small newsroom with no server capacity, with one important caveat: what you are monitoring becomes visible to MuckRock's infrastructure, so do not use it to watch pages whose monitoring would itself be sensitive (a target's site, a procurement portal in an active investigation). For public-interest watching of government pages it is excellent, and the automatic Internet Archive snapshot is a feature I would want even in a self-hosted setup.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-10, no releases, 9 stars, 1 open issue. Maintained as part of MuckRock's operated add-on ecosystem; repository metadata is thin because the service rather than the code is the artefact.
licence: BSD-3-Clause (add-on script); the front-end monorepo carries NO licence file, so its reuse rights are unverified
licence_restrictions: Add-on script is permissive. The extension and site code have no stated licence, so do not fork or redistribute those components without clarification.
costs: No direct fee; requires a DocumentCloud account (verified-journalist access has historically been free, with paid organisational tiers — current prices not verified in this survey). No infrastructure cost to you.
privacy: Watch configuration, run history and detected changes live in MuckRock's DocumentCloud infrastructure rather than the newsroom's. Internet Archive snapshots are public by design. Appropriate for monitoring public-interest pages; inappropriate where the fact of monitoring is sensitive.
alternatives: changedetection.io self-hosted, where monitoring must stay internal
Klaxon self-hosted for the same UX under your own control — but with maintenance caveats
webchanges plus Scoop for CLI monitoring with your own evidence capture
blockers: Hosted: monitoring activity and detected changes are visible to MuckRock infrastructure
summary: Hosted reimplementation of Klaxon as a DocumentCloud Add-On, with a browser extension for selecting page regions…
